PHSCS 587

Dopants and neutrality

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows which fixed and mobile charges must balance in a neutral bulk

Chemical doping counts impurity atoms, while electrical neutrality counts charges. Let ND and NA be total donor and acceptor concentrations. ND+ and NA− denote their ionized populations. A neutral homogeneous bulk satisfies n + NA− = p + ND+, since electrons and ionized acceptors contribute negative charge and holes and ionized donors contribute positive charge.

Complete ionization is an approximation, often useful for shallow dopants over an appropriate temperature and doping range. Then n − p = ND − NA, and equilibrium nondegenerate mass action supplies np = ni². Both equations are needed to determine n and p. Compensation matters: the net majority population can be far below either chemical dopant concentration.

At low temperature some carriers remain bound to dopants, producing freeze-out. Ionized populations then depend on dopant-level occupation, EF and T, and must be solved together with neutrality. At high temperature intrinsic carriers can dominate. Heavy doping may introduce degeneracy, impurity-band effects and bandgap changes, requiring a material-specific model.

Example

If fully ionized donors outnumber fully ionized acceptors by a factor of two, their difference supplies the net electron-minus-hole concentration. When that difference is much larger than ni, n is approximately ND − NA; the remaining holes follow equilibrium mass action.

Practice

1. Why can n ≈ ND fail even when all donors are ionized?

Include acceptors and intrinsic carriers.

Compensating acceptors reduce the net donor charge; intrinsic holes can also be appreciable. Full neutrality includes both carrier populations and both ionized dopant populations.

2. Does a neutral donor contribute to ND+?

Distinguish the chemical total from the charged subset.

A neutral donor belongs to ND but not ND+. Only its ionized positive charge enters the fixed donor-charge term.
